title: triprompt: deformation-aware multimodal prompting for robust 3D segmentation
desc: Accurate 3D medical image segmentation remains extremely challenging under severe anatomical variability caused by respiration motion, growth, and tumor-induced deformation. Existing prompt-based strategies mainly rely on visual and textual cues that essentially capture what organs look like or what they mean, although they fail to model how organs deform, which is a key determinant of organ geometry. We propose triprompt, a prompt-adaptive segmentation framework that jointly integrates structural visual prompt derived from localized image features; medical text prompt encoding domain knowledge; and a novel Population-Level Deformation Prompt (PDP) that learns statistical organ deformation patterns from data through a compact latent representation. These three prompts are jointly fused via a query-centric triprompt aligner, a lightweight alignment module that performs cross-prompt representation learning, allowing the segmenter to condition simultaneously on appearance, semantics, and physiological deformation. Empirical results on 11 public CT benchmarks show consistent gains in segmentation stability under extreme geometric shifts, underscoring the necessity of deformation-aware prompting for reliable, clinically actionable image segmentation. In order to promote reproducibility, our codes are open-sourced at: https://github.com/llmresearch678/triprompt.

title: Rubidium vapor cell spectroscopy by selective reflection approach
desc: Selective-reflection ellipsometry from miniaturized rubidium vapor cells is investigated numerically and experimentally as a phase-sensitive extension of conventional selective-reflection spectroscopy. While most previous studies of selective reflection have mainly focused on scalar reflectivity and line-shape analysis, the present work analyzes the reflected p- and s-polarized fields through the ellipsometric parameters $$\:{\Psi\:}$$ and $$\:{\Delta\:}$$. The reflected field from a finite rubidium vapor layer is calculated using a Fourier-series expansion of the coupled field–polarization equations for vapor-layer thicknesses ranging from $$\:L=\lambda\:/2$$ to $$\:L=9\lambda\:/4$$, where $$\:\lambda\:=795\:\text{n}\text{m}$$. The numerical results show that wavelength-scale changes in the vapor-layer thickness modify the selective-reflection spectrum and produce thickness-dependent resonant features. The calculated $$\:{\Psi\:}$$ and $$\:{\Delta\:}$$ spectra exhibit inverse-like behavior at complementary incidence angles, including $$\:{30}^{\circ\:}{,60}^{\circ\:}$$and $$\:{37}^{\circ\:},{53}^{\circ\:}$$. This behavior is interpreted as the combined result of angle-dependent optical path, wavelength-scale phase accumulation, Fabry–Pérot-type thin-layer interference, and resonant near-surface atomic polarization associated with selective reflection. Experimentally, the ellipsometric parameters are extracted from p- and s-polarized reflection measurements performed on a fabricated $$\:50\:\mu\:\text{m}$$ rubidium microcell. The experimental spectra support the physical observability of the complementary-angle ellipsometric response in a real miniaturized vapor-cell geometry. These results show that selective-reflection ellipsometry can provide a useful phase-sensitive approach for studying resonant optical responses in confined atomic vapor layers and offers a useful platform for compact spectroscopy, laser stabilization, and atom–surface interaction studies.

title: Immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and analgesic effects of Fasciola hepatica excretory/secretory proteins in a complete Freund’s adjuvant-induced rat model of rheumatoid arthritis
desc: Helminths can modulate immune responses by suppressing pro-inflammatory Th1/Th17 pathways and enhancing regulatory immunity, offering potential therapeutic benefits in autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). This study evaluated the anti-arthritic effects of excretory–secretory proteins (ESPs) from Fasciola hepatica in a Complete Freund’s Adjuvant (CFA)-induced RA rat model. Thirty male Wistar rats were assigned to five groups: healthy control, disease control, methotrexate-treated, prophylactic ESP, and therapeutic ESP. Rats in the ESP-treated groups received a cumulative intraperitoneal dose of 0.912 mg of F. hepatica ESPs. Over 28 days, clinical, behavioral, biochemical, and histopathological parameters were assessed. ESP treatment significantly reduced arthritis scores and paw edema (P < 0.05) and alleviated thermal and cold hypersensitivity (P < 0.001). Immunologically, ESP treatment promoted an anti-inflammatory immunoregulatory cytokine profile, characterized by increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) (P < 0.05) and reduced interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) levels (P < 0.01), supporting its proposed immunomodulatory mechanism. In serum, nitric oxide (NO) and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were significantly reduced, indicating improved oxidative status, while liver homogenates showed no significant changes for several markers. PET-CT imaging demonstrated reduced inflammatory activity, and histopathological findings confirmed joint protection, with mild hepatic and splenic alterations. These findings indicate that F. hepatica ESPs exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and analgesic effects in experimental RA and may represent a promising immunomodulatory strategy for experimental arthritis, although further mechanistic and safety studies are required.
